hero.summary: Senior Full Stack Engineer with 5+ years building scalable, cloud-native, and AI-powered applications. I work daily with React, Next.js, TypeScript, Node.js, Python, PostgreSQL, microservices, and AWS, integrating LLMs, AI APIs, and automation into production systems, with a focus on architecture, cloud infrastructure, CI/CD, and technical leadership.

start.title: How it started
paragraphs: My path into programming began in 2017, when I enrolled at Universidad Tecnológica de Santiago (UTESA) to study Systems Engineering. That is where I wrote my first lines of code and realized this was for me, understanding how things work under the hood and building them from scratch.

My first language was C#. It taught me the fundamentals I still rely on today: types, data structures, object-oriented design, and the discipline of writing code someone else can read. Then came JavaScript, and with it the web: suddenly I could build something, open it in a browser, and put it in anyone's hands.

In November 2020, while still studying, I started working as a freelance web developer on platforms like Upwork and Workana. That was two and a half years of turning designs into working sites, wiring front-end to back-end, and learning to work with real clients. That combination — the solid grounding of C# and the reach of JavaScript — shaped the rest of my career, and it is why I work comfortably on both sides of the stack today.

academy.title: Alterna Academy and finding a mentor
paragraphs: In 2022 I joined Alterna Academy, a programming school that marked a clear before and after. University gave me the theory and freelancing gave me the craft, the academy taught me how real software gets built as a team, with the practices and pace the industry demands.

That is where I met Eduardo Burgos, a software engineer with more than 20 years in the field and CEO of Alterna Academy. He was my mentor, he is someone I look up to, and today he is also a good friend. Much of how I think about development — making technical decisions with judgment, reviewing code honestly, teaching whoever comes next — comes straight from him.

Shortly after, in April 2023, I joined ProDoctivity SRL as a fullstack developer: my first formal role inside a product team, working with React, TypeScript, Node, Docker, and microservices. I graduated from UTESA in 2024, and alongside that I added projects at IMarket, where I also took on technical leadership.

I stayed at ProDoctivity until September 2025, the last few years as a senior fullstack developer, and there my work moved toward applied AI: I built a RAG-based document assistant on OpenAI LLMs, automatic document classification, and a standalone MCP service in Rust wired into the Node backend. Since September 2025 I have also led the technical side of Higher Bit Solutions as a contractor.

utesa.title: Giving back at UTESA
paragraphs: I had the honor of taking part in a tech event at Universidad Tecnológica de Santiago (UTESA), where I spoke about how to land your first job in tech, what a developer's day-to-day actually looks like, and a bit about my own path.
As a graduate of both UTESA and Alterna Academy, being able to share my experience and learning with people starting their careers in tech meant a lot to me.

All of it was possible thanks to Juan José Días Nerio, director of the Software Engineering program at UTESA and one of my great teachers, whose support and vision made the experience genuinely rewarding.
I shared the stage with outstanding professionals, and it was incredible to see the passion and experience each of them brought.

today.title: Why I do it
paragraphs: Events like that one remind me why I love what I do, and how much it matters to share knowledge, inspire, and connect with other professionals. It was a rewarding experience I would gladly repeat.
I still work with the same idea I started with: build things that genuinely work, learn from people who know more than I do, and give back some of what I received to those just getting started.

Outside of code I'm a gym rat: I've been training for 9 years without a break. The discipline the gym asks for, showing up every day even when I don't feel like it, is the same one I bring to my work. That's where Fitora came from: I wanted an app that built my routines and macros from clear rules, so I built it.

stockhex.name: StockHex - Inventory Management System
stockhex.description: Full-stack inventory management system with complete audit trail, built on a single domain invariant: stock is never edited directly. The only way to change it is to record a movement, and movement + stock are persisted in a single transaction, so history and quantities cannot drift apart and every change is attributed to its author; a mistake is never deleted, it is corrected by recording its reverse movement. The API follows clean architecture in four layers (Domain with no external dependencies, use cases returning Result<T> that never know about HTTP, controllers with no logic) and implements permission-based authorization, with roles editable as data and 31 permissions across 9 modules declared from a single source in code. It also ships JWT sessions with rotating refresh tokens and reuse detection, optimistic concurrency over rowversion with retries, and errors normalized as ProblemDetails (RFC 7807). Backed by 201 API tests —including tests against a real SQL Server via Testcontainers— and 418 E2E checks in a real browser with Playwright.
tasks: Designed an audit trail that cannot drift: a single SaveChanges stores the movement and the new stock with chained StockBefore/StockAfter, FKs set to Restrict so no cascade delete can wipe history, and a filtered unique index in the database that makes reverting the same movement twice impossible

Implemented dynamic RBAC with no permissions table: roles are data editable from the UI and permissions are declared in code next to the endpoint that requires them; the JWT carries only the role id and permissions are resolved per request with an invalidatable cache, so revoking a permission takes effect immediately without signing anyone out
Added a privilege-escalation guard: nobody can grant a permission they do not hold themselves

Hardened sessions: rotating refresh tokens stored only as SHA-256, reusing an already-rotated token invalidates the whole chain, per-IP rate limiting on /api/auth with 429 + Retry-After, and immediate lockout of deactivated accounts even though the JWT itself is not revocable

Solved concurrency with rowversion on the product plus retries using exponential backoff and jitter, verified against a real SQL Server in Testcontainers: 25 concurrent movements on the same product end in 25 successes and an exact stock value (that test caught a bug the InMemory provider could never reproduce)

Built a frontend derived from the backend with React 19 + TanStack Query: menu, buttons and routes come from the permission catalog exposed by the API, never from the role name; filters, search and pagination live in the URL, and the HTTP client guarantees a single token refresh in flight so simultaneous 401s cannot rotate the same refresh token and drop the session

Reduced deployment to one command: docker compose up -d --build brings up database, API and frontend, applies migrations and seeds the administrator; nginx serves the SPA and proxies /api (single origin, no CORS to configure) and the API URL is resolved at container startup, so the same image works in any environment

Covered the app with 201 API tests (xUnit, FluentAssertions, WebApplicationFactory, Testcontainers) and 6 E2E suites in real Chromium with Playwright —418 checks—, one of them dedicated to abusing the app: double clicks, back button, refreshes mid-flow, tampered URLs, six tabs at once and six viewport widths between 1920 and 390 px, auditing every screen for console errors, 5xx responses and layout overflow
Set up CI on GitHub Actions that builds with -warnaserror at zero warnings and audits vulnerable dependencies, including transitive ones

fitora.name: Fitora - Fitness & Nutrition App
fitora.description: Fitness app for iPhone and Android that assesses the user's physical condition, calculates calories and macros, and generates personalized training routines from explicit, deterministic rules and a reviewed exercise library: the same input always produces the same plan, and every proposal is validated before it reaches the user. Built as a monorepo with a pure Kotlin domain, a Spring Boot + PostgreSQL REST API deployed on Render, and a single React Native + Expo codebase for both platforms. The Android APK is published on Uptodown and the landing page is public; the source code is private.
tasks: Designed a monorepo under Hexagonal/Clean Architecture enforced by the build: the Kotlin domain fails to compile if it declares framework dependencies, ArchUnit validates the backend layers, and dependency-cruiser validates the app layers

Built the rules engine in pure Kotlin: BMR with Mifflin-St Jeor or Katch-McArdle, daily expenditure, calorie target with a safety floor and macro split, cardio calories via MET, estimated 1RM (Epley), and a routine generator (PPL, Full Body, Upper/Lower, Weider) that filters by equipment, injuries and level and validates weekly volume and recovery
Guaranteed rule parity between the Kotlin backend and the TypeScript app with shared golden cases (contracts/parity) run on both sides, keeping the server as the source of truth
Developed a single React Native + Expo app for iPhone and Android with layered architecture (domain, application, data, features), expo-router, i18n (Spanish/English), and API DTOs validated with Zod
Implemented offline training: the active plan lives in SQLite, every set is saved instantly and survives app restarts, and completed sessions are queued and synced when the connection returns

Integrated Gemini AI only on the backend, behind a per-feature port, for internet food search and daily menu proposals, with every response validated against domain rules and the app working fully without it

Hardened security: 15-minute JWTs with rotating refresh tokens and reuse detection, single-use 6-digit codes stored as HMAC with lockout after 5 attempts (no token ever travels in a link), rate limiting, RFC 9457 errors, session in Keychain/Keystore, recorded consent, and account deletion
Deployed the Spring Boot API with Docker and Flyway migrations on Render with managed PostgreSQL, signed and published the Android APK on Uptodown, and launched a public landing page

aijobhunter.name: AI Job Hunter - Personal Job Search Assistant
aijobhunter.description: Personal-use application (single user, runs on my own machine with Docker; it is not a public product and the code is private). I built it because searching for remote work by hand meant checking the same job boards every day, re-reading offers that did not fit (on-site only, unrealistic English requirements, below my salary floor) and losing track of who I had applied to and who had answered. AI Job Hunter searches authorized sources three times a day, analyzes each offer with AI against my real profile, discards what does not fit before spending tokens, ranks the rest by compatibility, freshness and number of applicants, and tracks every application from the first contact to the offer. It never applies or sends anything on its own: "Apply now" only opens the original offer. Built in 10 phases in a TypeScript monorepo (Next.js + NestJS) with hexagonal architecture and more than 60 architecture decisions recorded with their reasoning.
tasks: Why AI only extracts and a deterministic engine scores: the AI reads the offer and extracts facts, but the score (skills 30, experience 20, modality/location 15, salary 15, seniority 10, language 5, contract 5) is computed by pure domain code. That makes it testable, explainable and independent of the model; a criterion with no data (e.g. unpublished salary) is excluded instead of penalized, and any figure the AI returns that is not literally in the offer text is discarded

Why a "never invent" rule in the domain: anything the AI proposes from my CV that does not appear literally in it is dropped and shown to me, and nothing is saved until I confirm it. Prompts alone cannot guarantee this, so it is enforced in code; the same grounding applies to the AI-generated tailored CVs, cover letters, recruiter messages and follow-ups, which are drafts that are never sent automatically

Why only official sources: jobs come from public APIs, RSS feeds and ATS boards (Get on Board, Remotive, Remote OK, Himalayas, We Work Remotely, Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby) with per-source rate limits and attribution. LinkedIn, Indeed, Wellfound, Arc.dev and Workana prohibit scraping, so they are supported only through manual import; the app never bypasses CAPTCHAs or anti-bot protection, and availability checks respect robots.txt and block SSRF

Why exclusion filters run before the AI: on-site or hybrid offers, countries without work authorization and blocked companies are filtered with structured data first, so they never consume tokens. Gemini is the default provider because it is free for bulk analysis, Claude can be selected per task, and every AI call goes through a gateway with a 24-hour token budget and usage log

Designed a hexagonal monorepo (pnpm + Turborepo): business logic lives in a pure TypeScript core package with zero npm dependencies, adapters for Prisma, AI providers and job sources live outside it, the web only imports shared Zod contracts, and dependency-cruiser fails the build if any of these rules is broken

Built the backend with NestJS, Prisma 7 and PostgreSQL 17: three-way dedupe (source + id, normalized URL, company + title across sources), salaries kept exactly as published and converted to monthly USD with daily exchange rates, filtering, sorting and pagination in parameterized SQL, and RFC 9457 errors in a single format

Moved long-running work to a background worker with Redis + BullMQ: scheduled searches at 08:00, 13:00 and 18:00 in my time zone, a weekly check of whether open offers are still available, job state persisted so it survives restarts, and a partial unique index that prevents duplicate AI runs

Built the dashboard with Next.js 16, React 19 and Tailwind 4: daily goal, 10 indicators, "apply first" list, application tracking with 15 states, recruiter contact log and response metrics, analytics by period with server-rendered accessible charts (no chart library), company directory with favorites and blocked companies, notifications, and Spanish/English UI

Secured it as a single-user app: no sign-up endpoint (the owner is created by a script), opaque session cookie stored hashed in Postgres instead of JWT for real logout, argon2 passwords, protected routes by default, API keys only on the server, and contact data never sent to the AI

Backed it with Vitest unit tests and API integration tests against a real PostgreSQL via Testcontainers (no network access allowed in tests), with connectors tested against trimmed real fixtures, and CI on GitHub Actions
